s: Bei Sturm darf ein Kran nicht umfallen.
A crane must not fall over in the event of a storm.
Der Kran in der Küche tropft.
The tap in the kitchen is dripping.
Kran.et:
From Middle High German krane, from Old High German krano (“crane”), from Proto-West Germanic *kranō, from Proto-Germanic *kranô (“crane”).
The word was used metaphorically for the lifting device due to the similar appearance of the bird’s neck and head. This …

Kranich.et: From Middle High German kranech, from Old High German chranuh, from Proto-West Germanic *kranuk, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *kranô (“crane”).

Kranz.et:
From Middle High German kranz, from Old High German kranz, of uncertain origin, but probably related to the root of Kringel (“loop, curl”).
An exclusively High German word (compare e.g. Luxembourgish Kranz, Vilamovian kraonc). From Middle High German are borro…

Krankheit.et:
From Middle High German krancheit, krankeit. By surface analysis, krank + -heit; compare Alemannic German Chranket, Luxembourgish Krankheet.
Eclipsed non-native Middle High German malāze (“sickness, disease”), ultimately from Latin.
